notes.title: Operating system concept
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- OS = a resource manager.
- Layers: hardware → kernel → syscalls → utilities → shell → user.
- Kernel: interrupts, memory, CPU sharing.

---

*Linux_History_BasicCommands.ppt — "Operating System Concept".*

**OS = a resource manager.** It lets programs use the CPU, memory, disks and devices safely.

## The layers (bottom → top)
Hardware → **Kernel** → System call library → System utilities / applications → **Shell or GUI** → Users

## What the kernel does
- Handles interrupts from devices
- Gives memory to programs
- Shares the CPU between programs
- Offers **system calls** to the layers above

OSes differ in their system calls, utilities, user interface and scheduling.

notes.title: History of UNIX and Linux
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- MULTICS → UNIX (Thompson, Ritchie) → C in 1973.
- Linux: Linus Torvalds, 1991, free and open source.
- GNU = GNU's Not Unix.

---

*History deck; LinuxArchitecture_Distributions.pptx slides 1–3; Lab 1 Q1.*

## Timeline
| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| late 1960s | **MULTICS** (GE + MIT + Bell Labs) |
| ~1969 | Ken Thompson writes **UNICS → UNIX** |
| 1973 | UNIX kernel rewritten in **C** (Thompson + Dennis Ritchie) |
| 1978 | UNIX splits into **System V** and **BSD** |
| **1991** | **Linus Torvalds** releases the Linux kernel |

Linux follows **POSIX** and is a mix of SysV and BSD.
**GNU = "GNU's Not Unix"**.

## UNIX vs Linux
| UNIX | Linux |
|---|---|
| proprietary, needs a licence | free, open source |
| Bourne shell (sh) | bash by default |
| servers, mainframes | everything: phones to supercomputers |

notes.title: Linux distributions
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Distro = kernel + utilities + GUI + apps.
- Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Mint, openSUSE.
- GUIs: GNOME, KDE.

---

*LinuxArchitecture_Distributions.pptx slides 4–5.*

**Distribution (distro) = Linux kernel + system utilities + GUI + applications.**

- 600+ distros exist.
- Examples: **Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Linux Mint, openSUSE**, Manjaro, MX Linux, elementary, Solus, Deepin.
- GUIs: **GNOME, KDE**.
- Apps: Firefox, LibreOffice, vim, gcc.

notes.title: Linux architecture
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- 4 layers: hardware, kernel, shell, applications.
- Kernel = the core (memory, process, devices, syscalls).
- Shell = command interpreter (bash).

---

*LinuxArchitecture_Distributions.pptx slides 6–11; history deck "Architecture of Linux". This answers Lab 1 Q2.*

## Draw this (4 layers)
```
   Users
 ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ Applications / utils │  ls, grep, Firefox, LibreOffice
 ├──────────────────────┤
 │ Shell                │  bash, sh, ksh, csh, zsh
 ├──────────────────────┤
 │ Kernel               │  memory, process, device, syscalls
 ├──────────────────────┤
 │ Hardware             │  CPU, RAM, disk, I/O
 └──────────────────────┘
```

| Layer | Job |
|---|---|
| **Hardware** | physical parts; drivers talk to it |
| **Kernel** | the core: memory management, process management, device drivers, system calls and security. Lives at `/boot/vmlinuz` |
| **Shell** | takes your commands and passes them to the kernel |
| **Applications** | programs users run |

**Kernel types:** monolithic (Linux), micro, hybrid, exo.
**Shells:** bash (**B**ourne **A**gain **SH**ell), sh, ksh, csh/tcsh, zsh.

notes.title: Principles, file types, directories
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Everything is a file; case-sensitive.
- 4 file types: ordinary, directory, device, link.
- /etc config, /home users, /bin commands, /tmp temp.

---

*History deck: "Basic Principals" to "Summary: Directory Structure".*

## Basic principles
- **Everything is a file**
- Small programs that do one job well, chained with pipes
- Settings are stored in text files
- **Case-sensitive**

## 4 file types
Ordinary · Directory · Device · Link (**hard** = another name for the same file; **soft** = a shortcut that breaks if the target is deleted)

## Directories (root is `/`)
| Dir | Holds |
|---|---|
| `/bin` | user commands (ls, cp) |
| `/sbin` | admin (root) commands |
| `/boot` | boot files, the kernel |
| `/dev` | device files |
| `/etc` | **configuration files** |
| `/home` | users' home folders |
| `/root` | root user's home |
| `/lib` | shared libraries |
| `/mnt`, `/media` | mount points |
| `/proc` | live system info (virtual) |
| `/tmp` | temporary files (anyone can write) |
| `/usr` | user programs and libraries |
| `/var` | logs and changing data |

notes.title: Paths, internal/external commands, metacharacters
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Absolute starts with /, relative doesn't.
- Internal = built into the shell (cd); external = a program (ls).
- * any, ? one, > overwrite, >> append, | pipe.

---

*History deck "Absolute & Relative Paths"; Lab 1 Q4–Q6.*

## Login
Text login (virtual console) or graphical login. Username + password. Every user gets a home directory.

## Paths
| Absolute | Relative |
|---|---|
| starts with `/` | no `/` at the start |
| full path from root | from where you are now |
| `/home/user/Btech` | `Btech/FirstYear`, `../notes` |

## Internal vs external commands
| Internal (built-in) | External |
|---|---|
| part of the shell | separate program on disk |
| `cd`, `echo`, `alias`, `pwd` | `ls`, `grep`, `cp` |
| `type cd` → "shell builtin" | `type ls` → `/bin/ls` |

## Metacharacters
| Char | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | any characters | `*.txt` |
| `?` | exactly one character | `file?.txt` |
| `[ ]` | one from a set | `file[1-3]` |
| `>` / `>>` | write / append output to a file | `ls > a.txt` |
| `<` | input from a file | `sort < a.txt` |
| `|` | pipe output into the next command | `ls | wc -l` |
| `;` | run one after another | `cd /; ls` |
| `&` | run in the background | `sleep 10 &` |

## Linux vs Windows (not in any handout)
| Linux | Windows |
|---|---|
| free, open source | paid, closed |
| case-sensitive files | not case-sensitive |
| `/` single tree | drive letters C:, D: |
| strong CLI (bash) | GUI first |
| fewer viruses, more secure | more malware targets |

notes.title: Basic commands
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- ls, cd, pwd, mkdir, rmdir, touch, cat, cp, mv, rm.
- ls -l details, -a hidden, -h readable sizes.
- ps, top, free, df, du, uname, whoami for system info.

---

*linux basic commands.docx; history deck "Basic Linux Commands".*

| Command | Does | Useful options |
|---|---|---|
| `ls` | list files | `-l` details, `-a` hidden, `-h` sizes, `-t` newest first, `-R` recursive, `-d` the dir itself |
| `pwd` | show the current folder | |
| `cd` | change folder | `cd ..` up, `cd -` back, `cd ~` home |
| `mkdir` | make a folder | |
| `rmdir` | remove an **empty** folder | |
| `touch` | make an empty file / update its time | |
| `cat` | show or join files | |
| `cp` | copy | `-r` for folders |
| `mv` | move or rename | |
| `rm` | delete | `-i` ask, `-r` folders, `-f` force |
| `man` | the manual page | `man ls` |
| `echo` | print text | `echo $HOSTNAME` |
| `whoami` / `id` | the current user / user and group ids | |
| `ps` / `top` | running processes / live view | `ps aux` |
| `free -m` | memory use | |
| `df -h` / `du -sh` | disk space / folder size | |
| `uname -a` | system info | |
| `cal`, `date`, `clear`, `sort` | calendar, date, clear screen, sort lines | |

**cp/mv rule:** if the destination is a folder, the file goes inside it. If it's a file, it's overwritten. If it doesn't exist, the copy gets that new name.

notes.title: Installing Linux in a VM
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- VirtualBox (UTM on Mac) + Ubuntu ISO.
- Half the RAM, 20 GB+ disk.
- VM = safe, isolated, easy to test and back up.

---

*Installing Linux Using a Virtual Machine.pdf.*

## Steps (VirtualBox + Ubuntu)
1. Install **VirtualBox** (or VMware, Hyper-V; **UTM** on an Apple-silicon Mac).
2. Download the **Ubuntu LTS ISO**.
3. **New VM** → name → pick the ISO.
4. Set a username, password and hostname.
5. Give it **half your RAM** (8 GB of 16) and CPUs.
6. Disk: **at least 20 GB**.
7. Finish → it installs → set a password.
8. Optional: **Guest Additions** for full screen:
   `sudo apt update` → `sudo apt install -y build-essential linux-headers-$(uname -r)` → Devices → Insert Guest Additions → `sudo ./VBoxLinuxAdditions.run` → reboot.

## Why use a VM (benefits)
Better hardware use · safe and isolated · easy to scale · cheaper · good for testing · easy backup/recovery · easy to move.

notes.title: Lab record format
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A4, Times New Roman 12, left margin 1.5".
- Footer: URN + CSE2107 on every page.
- Live, full-window screenshots with your URN visible.

---

*Lab File format.docx.*

- **A4**, portrait. Margins: left **1.5"**, others 1".
- **Times New Roman.** Heading 14 pt bold, sections 12 pt bold, body 12 pt, justified, 1.15 spacing.
- Code in **Consolas / Courier New**, 10–11 pt.
- Each experiment starts on a **new page**: title (with COs), numbered steps/commands, output.
- **Footer on every page** (except the title page): your URN + course code **CSE2107**.

## Screenshot rules
1. **Live** screenshots from the lab only (no typed, copied or AI output).
2. Your **name or URN must be visible** in every screenshot.
3. **Full window**: the command and its result.

## SOPs
Bring the hard copy of the last experiment to the next lab for signing. Upload a scanned copy to **DigiiCampus** before the end-sem practical. Minimum **5 quizzes + 5 vivas**.
